name: Non-Linear Factor Models
title: Non-Linear Factor Models
answer: Non-linear factor models extend the linear factor framework by allowing a factor's effect on returns to depend on other factors, on the level of the factor itself, or on the market regime. In quantitative trading they are used to forecast cross-sectional returns, decompose risk, and build portfolios, often where simple linear regressions leave predictable structure unexplained. The site tracks 117 listed AI-related instruments with daily prices, and these models can be applied to such a universe alongside traditional equity factors. They sit within the broader AI Economist coverage of quantitative methods, not as a separate asset class.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on a data stack that provides point-in-time prices, fundamentals, and alternative data, because look-ahead bias will corrupt any factor model. Compute ranges from standard CPUs for tree-based methods to GPUs for neural networks, with cloud or on-premise clusters for large hyperparameter searches. Common software includes Python with scikit-learn, XGBoost, LightGBM, PyTorch, and TensorFlow, plus backtesting and portfolio construction libraries. The site's catalogue of 732 AI tools includes several libraries that support these pipelines, though the core requirement is clean, versioned data rather than any single package.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Practitioners start by engineering features from raw data, then split the sample with walk-forward or purged cross-validation to respect time order. They fit models such as random forests, gradient boosted trees, kernel regressions, or neural networks, tuning hyperparameters and applying regularization to control overfitting. Evaluation focuses on out-of-sample information coefficient, portfolio turnover, drawdown, and capacity, not just in-sample fit. Interpretability tools like SHAP values and partial dependence plots help check whether the model is learning sensible economic relationships. The final model is often blended with a linear factor model, which serves as a transparent benchmark.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Data rights and provenance are central, because alternative datasets may carry licensing restrictions, privacy obligations, or terms that forbid use in trading. Model risk management requires documentation, version control, audit trails, and a clear owner for each production model, especially when non-linear models are hard to explain to a risk committee. Regulators expect firms to avoid data snooping, look-ahead bias, and market manipulation, and to demonstrate that a strategy's signals are not derived from material non-public information. The site's 223 compliance and regulation pages cover many of these obligations for AI-related finance. There is no single rulebook for non-linear factor models, so practice varies by jurisdiction and by the nature of the data.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward models that combine non-linear flexibility with economic structure, such as hybrid factor models, causal machine learning, and interpretable neural networks. More alternative data and cheaper compute will keep expanding the feature space, but the risk of overfitting and the need for explainability will push back. Expect greater use of automated feature engineering and model monitoring, alongside continued reliance on linear factors as a baseline. Regulatory attention to AI in finance is likely to grow, and the site's 686 glossary terms will probably expand as new methods enter common use. The core tension, between predictive power and robustness, is unlikely to disappear.
